lines.t: A million-dollar ad budget.
A celebrity shoutout.
We assume that's what going viral costs.
It isn't.
Jonah Berger found six ingredients behind what spreads.
Here they are.
Social currency.
We share what makes us look in the know.
New York's Please Don't Tell bar hid its entrance in a hot dog shop phone booth, and the secret itself spread the word.
Triggers.
Ideas spread when everyday cues remind us.
Say peanut butter, and you think jelly.
Mars bar sales reportedly jumped when NASA's Pathfinder rover hit the news.
Emotion.
In a study of nearly seven thousand New York Times articles, awe and anger made stories more likely to be shared.
Sadness made them less likely.
Public.
We copy what we can see.
Apple turned its laptop logo to face outward, so every open laptop became a billboard.
Make the choice visible, and people imitate it.
Practical value.
People share useful news.
In that same study, more useful articles were shared more.
Make it quick, clear, and worth saving.
Stories.
In 2006, Blendtec spent fifty dollars on supplies for its first video: a CEO in a lab coat asking, will it blend?
Marbles, golf balls, then an iPhone.
The series passed one hundred fifty million views, and the company says retail blender sales rose seven hundred percent in two years.
The product was the story.
Social currency, triggers, emotion, public, practical value, stories.
You don't need all six, but each one raises the odds.
So before you post, ask why someone would look good sharing this.
Virality isn't luck.
It's design.
